items.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier AI model with advanced cybersecurity and long-horizon engineering capabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Gemini 4 Carbon: Our next frontier model
items.summary:
Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon, its most powerful AI model to date, featuring state-of-the-art cybersecurity performance and enhanced abilities for complex, long-duration engineering tasks. The model leads benchmarks in vulnerability detection, exploitation, and patching, and shows significant improvements in generating secure code and reducing errors in live coding environments.

Building on the recently released Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon is designed for sustained agentic workflows and excels in multi-step engineering challenges. Google is rolling out Carbon gradually through a controlled program with cybersecurity partners and plans to make it available to developers and businesses after further testing and refinement of safety measures.

Gemini 4 Carbon maintains a multi-layered safety and security framework, improving alignment and resilience against misuse. It is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, matching Argon's introductory pricing, with discounts for cached inputs.

items.title: Claude Code sends each background agent’s entire transcript to its model every 30 seconds to update status lines, consuming 15–20% of tokens by default since version 2.1.232 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude Code regularly sends each background agent’s transcript to its model
items.summary:
Claude Code periodically sends the full transcript of each background agent to its own model to generate a brief status update, which only appears in the agents panel and does not affect the main conversation. This process, enabled by default since version 2.1.232, consumes approximately 15–20% of tokens, impacting rate-limit headroom rather than direct costs.

A community-developed Bun preload script disables this behavior by intercepting the timer responsible for these summary requests, effectively reducing token usage without modifying the Claude Code binary. Users can install this script globally by setting environment variables to preload it for all Claude Code processes and restarting the daemon and sessions to apply the change.

items.title: Surge AI launches DAYJOB: Tax benchmark evaluating AI agents on 50 professional tax assignments across eight tax practice areas [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Dayjob: Tax – evaluating AI agents on 50 professional tax assignments
items.summary:
Surge AI introduced DAYJOB: Tax, a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on complex professional tax tasks requiring specialized expertise and judgment. The benchmark includes 50 assignments covering individual, business, international, and corporate tax areas, testing agents on tax returns, workpapers, reviews, and client advice.

The assignments involve diverse materials such as PDFs, spreadsheets, and emails, simulating real-world tax workflows with input from tax experts who developed and reviewed the tasks. Early results show varying AI performance, with some agents identifying critical tax deadlines and others missing them, highlighting the challenge of professional judgment in AI tax assistance.

items.title: Bernstein launches open-source deterministic governance layer for AI agents with verifiable audit logs and Cloudflare integration [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Bernstein – open-source governance layer for AI agents
items.summary:
Bernstein has released an open-source governance layer for AI agents that uses a deterministic Python scheduler to run agents in parallel without involving a model in the coordination loop, ensuring byte-identical plan replays. The system enforces user-written policies as code and produces verifiable audit records, including HMAC-chained event logs and signed receipts that enable offline verification without rerunning the process.

The platform supports orchestration of multiple AI coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI across parallel git worktrees and integrates with Cloudflare services such as Workers, Durable Objects, R2, and D1 for managing agent workflows and state. Bernstein emphasizes evidence-based auditing over traditional reports, providing tamper-evident logs stored locally and tools for verifying the integrity and provenance of runs. The project is in beta and includes features like error handling improvements, plugin manifests, and a Muse Code adapter.

items.title: Cartesia.ai presents scaling laws and efficiency gains for hierarchical networks that learn tokenization end-to-end, showing up to 10x compute and data savings in language modeling [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Scaling Hierarchical Networks
items.summary:
Cartesia.ai explores hierarchical networks (H-Nets) as a new architecture that replaces traditional tokenization by dynamically chunking raw data within the model, enabling more efficient and general learning from bytes. Their research demonstrates that H-Nets achieve significant compute efficiency improvements—up to 3-5x in controlled settings and 10x in more flexible models—while exhibiting novel behaviors like in-context tokenization.

The team highlights H-Nets' potential beyond language modeling, with ongoing work in biology and vision suggesting these architectures could serve as a general-purpose approach across modalities. This work aligns with the "bitter lesson" philosophy of learning directly from raw data and represents a step toward more scalable and data-efficient AI systems.

items.title: Sean Goedecke says mastering AI requires time and practice to develop durable skills beyond simple tricks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Getting good at AI takes time and practice
items.summary: Sean Goedecke argues that becoming proficient with AI involves more than just knowing tricks; it requires developing long-term skills through experience. He highlights common pitfalls for new users, such as expecting AI to understand vague requests without sufficient context, and emphasizes the importance of understanding what AI models can and cannot do. Goedecke also discusses the unique challenges of reviewing AI-generated code and the skill of quickly skimming AI output to find useful information. He acknowledges that while future AI improvements may reduce some learning barriers, currently effective AI use demands ongoing practice and skill development.

items.title: Anthropic launches Claude smart reports for managers to track employee AI usage and identify off-topic work communications [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude's new smart reports tell bosses when workers are 'off-topic'
items.summary:
Anthropic has introduced smart reports in its AI assistant Claude, enabling managers to monitor how employees use the AI tools and detect off-topic or personal discussions during work. The feature is available to paid Claude Enterprise users and generates interactive charts summarizing team activity, spending, and output types over customizable date ranges.

The reports analyze conversation transcripts to group workstreams and classify sessions by productivity and relevance, highlighting inefficiencies and obstacles. While Anthropic emphasizes that these reports are not intended for evaluating individual performance or employment decisions, the tool raises concerns about workplace surveillance and AI's role in monitoring employee behavior. Managers can also customize queries and receive recommendations to optimize AI usage within teams.

items.title: NVIDIA GeForce GPUs run matrix math at half the speed of professional cards using the same chip, with modders unlocking full speed on gaming cards [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GeForce vs. Workstation GPUs: Nvidia's Half Rate, Priced
items.summary: NVIDIA sells GeForce and professional GPUs based on the same silicon but limits GeForce cards to half the training speed for 32-bit sum matrix math, a setting confirmed by recent open-source Linux modules that unlock full speed. Tests show unlocked GeForce cards match professional card performance per clock cycle, proving the speed difference is a software cap rather than hardware limitation. Despite the cap, GeForce cards remain the most cost-effective option for matrix math workloads. The modules have limitations and risks, including some failures and incompatibility with newer Blackwell-generation GPUs like the RTX 5090, which uses different speed caps for various precision formats.

items.title: Research paper proposes a ledger-based model to measure AI time savings accounting for errors and validates it with developer studies and experiments on AI-assisted review workflows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
items.summary: The paper examines how to measure the time saved by AI assistance, contrasting a simple stopwatch approach with a ledger view that factors in errors allowed through. It introduces a model defining time saved and excess defects, proposing a break-even defect cost metric. The study replicates a developer study showing mixed AI impact on issue resolution speed and analyzes review workflows limiting GPT-5's speedup to 3.6 times. An experiment with AI reviewers checking AI-generated drafts found that reviewers adjusted effort based on perceived error rates, sometimes trading speed for accuracy.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.35942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I consider what it means for AI assistance to save time. I contrast a stopwatch view, on which time saved is whatever the clock records, with a ledger view, on which it is a counterfactual that has to be read next to the errors the work lets through, and I argue for the latter. The argument has four parts. I define a model-free pair of quantities, time saved and excess escaped defects, and one decision number built from them: the break-even defect cost. I give a baseline model of checking in which, until the model is good enough not to check, a calibrated worker's escaped-defect rate does not depend on how good the model is; checking time grows with the logarithm of the model's error rate; and over-trust buys minutes on the clock at a larger cost in total minutes. I show what randomized studies can and cannot identify, and I replicate METR's developer study from its public data: the same 246 issues support a slowdown of 19% or 24% depending on the estimand (34% without adjusting for a chance imbalance), and AI helped on somewhere between 3% and 82% of them. Finally, I restate the published record, with stated bounds in place of imported point assumptions. In GDPval's own review-every-output workflow, review time alone caps GPT-5's speedup at 3.6x; the consultants outside the frontier were faster, and more often wrong. Last, I test two of the model's predictions in a small pre-specified experiment on AI reviewers checking AI drafts of the same kind of brief, built from SEC filings made after the models' training data were collected. Told the drafter's true error rate, the reviewer checked more as it rose, but all-or-nothing, switching near where its prompt's costs break even. Told that the drafter erred ten times less often than it did, it checked 7 fewer of 9 figures and let a wrong figure through in 22.5% of briefs instead of none: faster and worse, entirely through reduced effort.

items.title: Researchers propose data generation strategies using augmentation and DCGANs to improve deep learning classification of olive tree diseases, demonstrating enhanced accuracy with EfficientNetV2B0 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Enhancing Deep Learning Model Performance through Data Generation Strategies: Classification of Olive Tree Diseases
items.summary: Researchers address limitations in deep learning for plant disease diagnosis caused by insufficient data and class imbalance by applying data generation techniques including traditional augmentation, CutMix, MixUp, and synthetic images from DCGANs. They test three scenarios of data distribution—balancing classes, increasing samples per class, and expanding balanced datasets—using the EfficientNetV2B0 model with pre-trained and fine-tuned weights, resulting in substantial accuracy improvements. The study highlights the importance of data diversity and class balance, offering a promising approach for enhancing dataset quality in plant disease detection and precision agriculture.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.35984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning models are highly effective in a wide range of domains, particu larly in plant disease diagnosis. However, their performance is often limited by challenges such as insufficient data and class imbalance. In our work, we propose a comprehensive data generation strategy to overcome these limitations. First, we apply various data generation techniques, including traditional augmentation methods, CutMix, MixUp, and synthetic image generation using Deep Convolu tional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs), to create new data samples. Second, we exploit this generated data in three scenarios: (S1) balancing class distribution in the original dataset, (S2) increasing the number of samples per class, and (S3) expanding the dataset while maintaining balanced classes. Third, we evaluate the impact of these data distributions (S1, S2, S3) on model perfor mance using the EfficientNetV2B0 architecture with pre-trained and fine-tuned weights. The experimental results show a substantial improvement in classifica tion accuracy, emphasizing the critical role of data diversity and class balance. These findings highlight the effectiveness and adaptability of the proposed strat egy of data generation and distribution for enhancing dataset quality, offering promising applications in plant disease detection and precision agriculture.

items.title: Researchers introduce The Trinity, a capability-driven recursive self-improvement framework for multimodal agents that reorganizes tasks into a hierarchical capability tree and evolves specialized modules [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
items.summary:
Researchers present The Trinity, a framework designed to improve multimodal agents by coupling world generation with Harness evolution through roles named Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. This approach shifts task organization from surface categories to shared capability requirements, enabling recursive self-improvement and better scalability across diverse tasks. The framework uses a Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real method to abstract common requirements into simplified simulated environments for capability learning, while evaluating transfer on original tasks.

The Trinity progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree with validated updates that accumulate over iterations. A Capability-Aware Harness Router selects compatible module configurations based on public task information. The evolved Harnesses demonstrate significant performance improvements, increasing mean scores by 34 points on 28 training benchmarks and 26 points on 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce CohortFlow, a steerable clinical cohort curation agent that uses localized semantic corrections to reduce latency and model calls while maintaining accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CohortFlow: A Steerable Clinical Cohort Curation Agent with Localized Semantic Correction
items.summary:
CohortFlow is a language model agent designed to update clinical cohort eligibility criteria efficiently by applying localized semantic corrections rather than reprocessing entire specifications. It uses a persistent execution graph with recorded semantic dependencies to selectively invalidate affected computations while preserving valid prior results, aiming to reduce correction latency and computational overhead.

In tests involving 100 scenarios from clinical-trial eligibility criteria with 126 correction turns, CohortFlow achieved a 77.0% requirement micro-F1 score compared to 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B parameter model, with no statistically significant difference. The approach reduced mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, and decreased model calls by 38.1%. A separate evaluation on the MIMIC dataset showed successful execution of all 13 cohort states and demonstrated selective recomputation of changed or dependent nodes, supporting the method's efficiency and accuracy.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model agents for clinical cohort curation should accommodate evolving eligibility criteria without repeatedly processing unchanged requirements. We introduce CohortFlow, a steerable agent that represents natural language corrections as localized updates to a structured cohort specification and reconciles them with a persistent execution graph. Explicitly recorded semantic dependencies enable affected computations to be selectively invalidated while preserving valid prior results. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria, comprising 126 correction turns, localized steering achieves 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B model, a small numerical advantage that is not statistically significant ($p=0.493$). It reduces mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept evaluation over MIMIC, all 13 cohort states execute successfully, while correction trajectories demonstrate selective preservation of unaffected computations and recomputation of changed or dependent nodes. Together, these results show that localized semantic steering can substantially reduce correction latency and model calls while maintaining strong requirement-level accuracy.

items.title: Researchers propose a framework for human-led science integrating AI by emphasizing durable human understanding and direction across all research phases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
items.summary:
As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers in core scientific tasks, this paper addresses why humans should continue doing science and how they should use AI in the process. It argues that science's essential goal is durable, collective human understanding pursued in service of human values, and proposes a two-part test for delegating research tasks to AI: ensuring the scientific community can explain and contest claims, and maintaining human judgment over research questions and interpretations.

The framework applies this test to all research phases using the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT), offering tailored recommendations for different fields. It differs from existing guidance by focusing on science's purpose rather than integrity norms, holding even if AI outperforms humans, and evaluating AI use based on its impact on human understanding and direction rather than tool type. The paper concludes with suggested reforms to preserve science's focus on human understanding and accountability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. It closes with the reforms needed to keep science aimed at human understanding and direction.

items.title: Researchers propose StruPO, a structure-aware prompt editor that uses calibrated scene graphs to improve faithfulness in text-to-image generation without iterative critique loops [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Structural Feedback to Prompt Policies: Learning Faithful Text-to-Image Prompt Editors
items.summary:
Researchers introduce StruPO, a prompt editor designed to optimize text-to-image prompts by preserving scene structure while enhancing image quality. StruPO uses calibrated scene graphs for policy conditioning and image-grounded supervision, enabling token-aligned prompt modifications through deletion, reordering, and insertion. This approach transforms structural feedback into a training signal for a reusable editing policy that handles uncertain grounding and stochastic image generation.

The team evaluated StruPO across three distinct 2,000-prompt test sets and four frozen generation backbones, comparing it to other prompt optimizers, structural feedback methods, diffusion-model fine-tuning, and attention control techniques. Results show consistent improvements in relational fidelity and a better balance between faithfulness and aesthetics. Independent automatic evaluators and a 15-annotator study confirmed these gains, with human preference increasing alongside relation complexity. Controlled ablations linked the improvements to graph conditioning, local editing, and image-grounded learning, with the final policy producing optimized prompts in a single pass after graph calibration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt optimization should improve the image a user receives without changing the scene the user requested. Yet stylistic rewriting can weaken object attributes and relations even when global text--image similarity remains high. We propose StruPO, a structure-aware prompt editor that uses a calibrated scene graph as a shared representation for policy conditioning and image-grounded supervision. The graph exposes what should be preserved, while deletion, reordering, and insertion provide a token-aligned way to modify the prompt. This turns structural feedback from an external critique into a training signal for a reusable editing policy. Learning from that signal requires handling both uncertain grounding and stochastic image generation. StruPO retains grounding confidence through smooth reward shaping and averages multiple images for each edit before computing group-relative advantages. Experiments span three disjoint 2K-prompt test sets and four frozen generation backbones, with comparisons to learned prompt optimizers, iterative structural feedback, diffusion-model fine-tuning, and inference-time attention control. StruPO improves the faithfulness--aesthetics trade-off, with consistent gains in relational fidelity. Independent automatic evaluators and a 15-annotator study provide complementary evidence, and human preference margins increase with relation complexity. Controlled ablations connect these gains to graph conditioning, local editing, and image-grounded learning. The resulting policy produces reusable optimized text in one pass after graph calibration, without an iterative critique--rewrite loop.

items.title: Researchers propose a decision-theoretic approach using priors to resolve conflicts between retrieval-augmented language model knowledge and retrieved context [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Don't Pick a Winner: Knowledge Conflicts Need a Prior, Not a Rule
items.summary:
A new study addresses how retrieval-augmented language models handle conflicts between their internal knowledge and retrieved context, which often disagree when the context is incomplete or incorrect. Existing methods use fixed rules to resolve these conflicts, but these rules fail when conditions vary. The researchers argue that resolving such conflicts requires separate evidence about each source and a prior on the reliability of the context, which current methods lack.

They tested their approach on the GRACE benchmark, which measures the accuracy of model knowledge and context separately. Their system, which incorporates calibrated confidence and a prior reflecting the true share of correct contexts, outperformed all baselines by up to 26 points across different context mixtures. The gains disappear when the model lacks knowledge, confirming theoretical predictions. This approach suggests that adaptive priors are essential for effectively combining multiple knowledge sources in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A retrieval-augmented language model answers from two sources, the retrieved context and its own knowledge, and the two disagree whenever the context is incomplete or wrong. Existing methods settle the disagreement with a rule fixed at design time: follow the context, amplify it in proportion to how far it moves the model, or trust the model's memory. Each rule is confidently wrong in some deployment. In a decision-theoretic model of two sources, the score of any fixed rule is linear in the share of reliable contexts while the best attainable score is convex, so every fixed rule is beaten wherever it is not exactly optimal; and a symmetric divergence between the two sources, the signal adaptive decoding uses, carries no information about which one is right. Resolving a conflict therefore needs two inputs that no existing method keeps: evidence about each source separately, and a prior on how often the context is right. We test these claims on GRACE, a benchmark that intervenes on the knowledge-graph context of a fixed question, so that what the model knows, what the context says and what is true are measured separately. There, every baseline from four families is strong on right contexts or on wrong ones, never on both. We then build the two inputs: the model states its knowledge as notes, a small policy voices each note with a calibrated confidence, a reader answers in two voices, and a selector commits or abstains under a prior $\pi$ applied as an exact prior shift. With $\pi$ set to the true share of right contexts, the system is above the best baseline at every mixture of GRACE contexts, by up to 26 points. Its overall score is 45.3 and 35.0 (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Llama-3.1-8B), against 29.4 and 27.5 for the best baseline. On preregistered ClashEval it beats same-backbone CK-PLUG and TCR by 12 and 26 points. Where the model lacks the knowledge, the gains vanish, as the theory predicts.

items.title: Researchers use quantile regression on FIFA World Cup 2022 tracking data to model player time-to-arrival, outperforming physics-based methods and testing transferability to basketball and NFL data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning Human Sports Motion Feasibility via Quantile Regression on Tracking Data
items.summary:
Researchers developed a model estimating the shortest plausible time a player needs to reach any location on the field, called time-to-arrival (TTA), by framing it as a conditional quantile regression problem. They trained a multilayer perceptron (MLP) on optical tracking data from all 64 matches of the FIFA World Cup 2022 and compared it against six existing player-motion models and a reachable-hull baseline, with the MLP consistently outperforming physics-based approaches.

To evaluate the model's generality, the team tested it on basketball and NFL tracking datasets, analyzing how well player motion dynamics transfer across different sports. The project and code are publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study time-to-arrival (TTA) in sports: the shortest plausible time a player needs to reach an arbitrary location on the pitch given their current kinematic state, estimated as the lower envelope of observed locomotion times. Rather than modeling space ownership through position density estimation or closed-form physics-based models, we cast TTA as a conditional quantile regression problem, estimating the lower quantile of locomotion time so the model learns a player's lower-envelope arrival time. We train the model on optical tracking data from all 64 matches of the PFF FC FIFA World Cup 2022 dataset, and evaluate a lightweight multilayer perceptron against six player-motion models from the literature, re-expressed as TTA predictors, and a learned reachable- hull baseline. Across our evaluation metrics, the MLP consistently outperforms every physics-based baseline. To probe the generality of the learned locomotion model, we further evaluate it on basketball tracking data and a single-game NFL tracking dataset, analyzing the transferability of player motion dynamics across sports. Our project is available at https://github.com/mguti97/TTA-Quantile.

items.title: Skill Dreaming framework learns and evolves repository-specific coding skills from pull request histories to guide continuous software development and maintenance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Skill Dreaming: Evolving Repository Skills through Pull Request Streams
items.summary:
Skill Dreaming is a framework that extracts and refines executable knowledge from validated pull requests (PRs) to build a repository-specific skill library for large language model agents. It leverages PR streams to capture evolving code structures, implementation patterns, and maintenance requirements, enabling coding agents to implement features while maintaining tests, documentation, and compatibility.

By integrating pull request analysis, skill management, code execution, and continuous integration, Skill Dreaming creates a feedback loop where PRs update skills and skills improve future PRs, supporting ongoing repository development and maintenance. This approach aims to automate and enhance complex software engineering tasks by continuously adapting to repository changes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on reusable skills for complex software engineering tasks, making skill libraries essential for repository development and maintenance. However, repository-specific skills must evolve with changing code structures, implementation conventions, and maintenance requirements. Pull requests (PRs) provide a natural source of such knowledge by recording how repositories evolve through implementation and review. Meanwhile, new PRs must follow repository-specific implementation patterns, modify related components consistently, and ensure that existing tests continue to pass while adding coverage for new functionality. This creates a mutually reinforcing cycle: PRs provide knowledge for updating skills, while these skills improve future PRs, maintain repositories, and support further skill evolution. To enable this co-evolution of PRs, repositories, and skills, we propose Skill Dreaming, a framework that learns from PR streams to guide continuous repository development and maintenance. Given a repository and its PR history, Skill Dreaming builds a repository-specific skill library by extracting executable knowledge from validated PRs and continuously refines the skills as new PR information becomes available. These skills guide coding agents not only in implementing requested features but also in maintaining associated tests, documentation, compatibility, and repository conventions. By integrating PR analysis, skill management, code execution, and continuous integration, Skill Dreaming provides an end-to-end workflow for applying learned skills to repository changes and incorporating subsequent PR outcomes into future skill updates.

items.originalTitle: MARQ: A Modular, LLM-Agnostic Requirement Quality Assessor Infused with Systems Engineering Knowledge
items.summary: MARQ is a prototype that enhances large language models (LLMs) with expert-derived systems engineering knowledge to better evaluate requirement quality based on INCOSE criteria. Tested on an expert-labeled NASA requirement dataset using Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemma 3 12B, MARQ achieved higher median F1 scores than baseline models, with improvements varying by model and quality criterion. The system showed particular gains in Correctness and Conformance but highlighted trade-offs between defect detection and false alarms, emphasizing the need for criterion-specific tuning and human oversight in requirement engineering support.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Requirements engineering (RE) is foundational to systems engineering (SE), as requirement defects can propagate downstream and adversely affect development outcomes. Although large language models (LLMs) are promising for requirement quality assessment, prior work shows that off-the-shelf models miss a large share of expert-identified defects, perform unevenly across quality criteria, and vary across executions. This study investigates whether infusing expert-derived SE knowledge can improve LLM-based requirement quality evaluation beyond off-the-shelf capability. We present MARQ, a modular, LLM-agnostic prototype that supplements LLMs with a criterion-specific knowledge stack operationalizing INCOSE requirement quality criteria and evaluated against off-the-shelf baselines on an expert-labeled NASA requirement set using Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the open-weight Gemma 3 12B, with 100 executions per model. MARQ achieves median F1 scores of 0.80 for Claude Opus 5, 0.62 for GPT-5.6 Sol, and 0.53 for Gemma 3 12B, compared with off-the-shelf baselines of 0.55, 0.52, and 0.18, respectively. However, the nature of these gains is model-dependent. Claude Opus 5 improves defect detection and false-alarm control; GPT-5.6 Sol gains detection and better execution-level consistency at the cost of more false alarms; and Gemma 3 12B reaches the performance of off-the-shelf proprietary models, although it remains highly variable. Criterion-level analysis shows gains concentrated in Correctness and Conformance, trade-offs between misses and false alarms within individual criteria, and model-dependent responses across several criteria. These findings position SE knowledge infusion as a promising model-agnostic pathway for strengthening trustworthy LLM-based RE support while underscoring the need for criterion-specific interventions and human-in-the-loop review.

items.summary: Researchers introduce BehaveRec, a sequential recommendation framework that integrates recent session data, a 90-day user history encoder, and a user-user graph based on behavioral similarity to improve prediction accuracy. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sequential recommendation models typically predict a user's next action from recent session interactions, which limits personalization when short-term signals are weak or ambiguous. Rather than assuming that incorporating longer-term history and community signals is universally beneficial, we study when it actually helps. We propose BehaveRec, a three-signal framework combining a causal session transformer, a bidirectional User History Encoder over a 90-day window, and a GraphSAGE module over a user-user graph built from behavioral embedding similarity rather than item co-occurrence; a learned gate blends the three signals per user. On an industrial dataset of 137M sequences from 12.6M users, BehaveRec improves R@5 by +3.2% over SASRec, with a larger-capacity SASRec baseline (more parameters than BehaveRec) still trailing by +2.5%, ruling out capacity as the explanation. More importantly, a user-level stratification by history length reveals a clear dose-response relationship: BehaveRec's advantage is negligible below roughly 10 interactions and grows monotonically with history richness, reaching +0.017 R@5 for users with 101+ events. This pattern is corroborated across one industrial and three public datasets spanning history-rich to history-sparse regimes, where session-only models remain preferable. These headline results, and the resulting deployment threshold, are established for category-level intent prediction; a preliminary, single-run check on the full item-level vocabulary yields a directionally mixed result and is scoped as an open question rather than a claim. We use these results to derive a practical deployment rule -- roughly 20 interactions per user -- for when long-term history and behavioral-graph signals are worth their added complexity. Despite this added complexity, BehaveRec remains lightweight: it uses 5.67M parameters and trains on a single GPU in under two days.

items.title: A Smart Instant Book Filter Model based on Dual-Objective Optimization [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: A Smart Instant Book Filter Model based on Dual-Objective Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hospitality service in online marketplaces has become increasingly popular over the past few years, not only because it helps people easily rent short-term lodging but also because it empowers travelers to connect with locals and feel belonging. A typical pattern of these industries is a central platform mediating the economic interactions between guests and hosts, where a successful booking experience is the key to user satisfaction. However, one of the biggest challenges is the possible delay of response and chance of rejection when guests try to book a request-to-book listing. Previously, we enabled the instant book feature to allow hosts to instantly accept qualified guests and guests to confirm bookings immediately. Yet the symptom has not been alleviated given mixed request-to-book and instant book listing supply in search results. One possible solution is to promote all instant book listings in search results; however, booking rate will be damaged due to some improperly promoted low quality listings. In this paper, we present a novel smart instant book filter system that applies the instant book filter intelligently and shifts request-to-book to instant book without hurting booking rate. Compared with traditional two-sided markets research that targets finding strategies to maximize a single overall social welfare goal, our proposed system aims to maximize the instant book rate with the constraint that booking rate should not decrease, forming a dual-objective optimization problem. We show A/B testing results for our system exposed to global users, demonstrating that our model performs better than previous human-expert-tuned models in terms of both instant book rate and overall booking rate. We also achieved improved metrics such as the host instant book adoption rate. The proposed system has been deployed to production and is serving millions of users every day.

items.title: Spiking Neural Networks Are Harder to Steal: A Benchmark Study of Model Stealing Attacks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Spiking Neural Networks Are Harder to Steal: A Benchmark Study of Model Stealing Attacks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning models deployed behind query interfaces expose more than their predictions, because an adversary can use those predictions to rebuild the model itself. Model stealing attacks (MSAs) exploit this exposure by training a surrogate model that replicates the decision behavior of a target through black-box queries alone, without access to its parameters or training data. These attacks are well characterized for conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs), yet spiking neural networks (SNNs) process information in a fundamentally different way. SNNs communicate through sparse, discrete spikes, and their outputs depend on membrane potentials that evolve over time rather than on a static mapping from input to output. This temporal mode of computation suggests that the decision behavior of an SNN may be harder to reconstruct from its responses. This work tests that possibility by benchmarking four representative MSAs, namely the Papernot, Tram\`er, T-RND, and color perturbation attacks, against SNNs and their ANN counterparts on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10. Across every attack and dataset, SNNs prove consistently more difficult to steal. Surrogates of SNNs achieve 10% to 20% lower agreement with the target model and 15% to 25% lower adversarial transferability than surrogates of ANNs. We attribute this resistance to the way SNNs compute, as their spike-based and time-dependent dynamics yield decision boundaries that ANN-based surrogates struggle to approximate, even under large query budgets. These findings extend the known resilience of SNNs beyond attacks on training data to the replication of model functionality, strengthening the case for neuromorphic architectures in security-sensitive applications.

items.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.

items.title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.

items.title: How Stable Are LLM-Generated Proofs Under Program Refactoring? A Stress Test for Verifiable Code Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Stable Are LLM-Generated Proofs Under Program Refactoring? A Stress Test for Verifiable Code Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36328v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Benchmarks for verifiable code generation usually test a proof against one fixed implementation. We ask whether the same proof remains valid after a program refactoring that preserves behavior. We introduce RefactorProof, which derives 458 Lean-certified variants from the 185 VERINA tasks that compile in our pinned environment while holding the specification and evaluated proof fixed byte-for-byte. VERINA supplies reference proofs for 46 tasks, all from its basic split; the primary model-versus-reference comparisons further match on 21-25 short, non-recursive tasks. Structural refactorings expose substantial brittleness across proof sources: task-normalized structural PSR is 4.3% for the supplied references and 13.3-26.8% for the specialized provers. items.title: Plenty of Room in the Middle: Revealing Opportunities on a GPU Cluster via Fine-Grained Monitoring [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Plenty of Room in the Middle: Revealing Opportunities on a GPU Cluster via Fine-Grained Monitoring
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GPU clusters have become essential computing resources for AI and scientific research in academia and industry. However, their high cost and growing demand often result in long queueing delays. While previous monitoring efforts have operated at second- or minute-level frequencies, they primarily informed job-level scheduling for clusters and lacked the detail needed to optimize GPU-level utilization. This paper presents an in-depth study of a university research GPU cluster, analyzing resource usage at 100 ms intervals. We have developed a lightweight monitoring tool that leverages Nvidia's DCGM library to capture fine-grained "compute utilization" metrics within GPUs. Deployed on a cluster with 89 nodes and 319 GPUs, our tool collected data over several months. This paper focuses on a 10-day period with 7,399 jobs submitted by 150 users from 12 departments. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) the GPU cluster exhibits significant underutilization, with over 70% of jobs using less than 20% of GPU memory and 50% averaging below 5% Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) utilization; (2) 80% of jobs have a drastic mismatch between their requested and actual durations, significantly limiting the scheduler's effectiveness; and (3) the multi-GPU jobs we examined show highly periodic communication patterns. These findings suggest there is plenty of room in the middle: substantial utilization gains are available through better job scheduling and GPU multitasking, independent of hardware or application improvements. Our monitoring solution is available as open-source software at https://github.com/als244/gpu_server_monitoring.

items.title: OA-RAG: Ontology-based Agentic RAG for Faithful LLM Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OA-RAG: Ontology-based Agentic RAG for Faithful LLM Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well across many real-world tasks but remain prone to hallucination, limiting their reliability in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare, where answers must be grounded in established knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates this problem by incorporating external information, but often overlooks logical relationships and relies heavily on the LLM's own reasoning, which can compromise answer faithfulness. We propose OA-RAG, an agent that integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning, drawing on both the logical structure and informal annotations of domain ontologies. For each answer, OA-RAG reports the ontology observations used as evidence and a model-assessed grounding level (entailed, supported, related, or unrelated) that characterises the strength of that evidence. Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical question-answering tasks, OA-RAG achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods, with particularly strong results on reasoning-intensive tasks. The reported grounding levels also offer a useful indication of answer reliability, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy. Finally, our results demonstrate the value of ontologies as knowledge sources: OA-RAG is competitive with, and sometimes outperforms, domain-specific RAG systems that draw on sources such as textbooks.

items.title: Executable Archaeology of Programs That Model Programming: Reanimating the Heuristic Compiler (1961) and KBEmacs (1984) [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Executable Archaeology of Programs That Model Programming: Reanimating the Heuristic Compiler (1961) and KBEmacs (1984)
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Early AI programs were often also theories of how people think, and programs that wrote programs were, in part, theories of how people program. Here we report on the reanimation of two such programs that offer two seemingly different theories of programming and were developed for quite different purposes. The first, Herbert Simon's Heuristic Compiler (1961), was an experimental model of programming as problem-solving, applying the means-ends analysis methods of the General Problem Solver to investigate the nature of the programming task. The second, KBEmacs (1984), was a working prototype of an intelligent programming assistant developed by MIT's Programmer's Apprentice project, built on the view that expert programmers recognize and combine familiar patterns, or "cliches." It let a programmer build up programs by combining cliches through a stylized English command language. We approach both through the methodology of Executable Archaeology, the study of historical computational systems by running their original code, a process we call "reanimation." Our reanimation of the Heuristic Compiler reproduces the compiled code appearing in Simon's 1963 paper, and our reanimation of KBEmacs reproduces the SQRT sequence of its December 1984 self-test. Examined side by side, the two theories turn out to have much in common: the Heuristic Compiler also works by adapting existing routines, and Simon later argued that search alone requires a large body of programming knowledge. To highlight the reflexivity of this project, we deliberately used a modern AI-assisted programming tool, Anthropic's Claude Code (Opus 5.5), to carry out much of the detailed reanimation work, building on a significant base of existing software. The explicit, executable theories of programming that both systems embodied are largely absent from today's far more capable AI coding assistants.

items.title: WAKMan: Workload Aware KVCache Manager [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WAKMan: Workload Aware KVCache Manager
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prefix caching enables a Large Language Model (LLM) servers to reuse the Key-Value (KV) states and accelerate prefill computation stage for requests that share a prefix with earlier prompts, thus reducing latency and serving cost. With limited memory resource, the KV cache eviction policy becomes a decisive factor in determining the overall benefits of prefix caching. Production traffic may have single-turn, multi-turn, agentic, or a mixture of any combination of these request types. Our findings indicate that agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency, while popular prompts and long conversations return after many other requests and favor frequency. Across 20 mixes, no single policy is always best: vLLM's default strategy LRU provides 12% higher cache hits as compared to the frequency-oriented S3FIFO on agentic-heavy mixes but trails it by up to 22% elsewhere, and even a single workload parameter can flip the winner even for any particular mix. We present WAKMan, a workload-aware KV cache manager that picks its eviction policy from live traffic without knowing request types or reading prompts. It improves hit rate over LRU by 5 percentage points on average, with the lowest mean and worst-case optimality gap of all policies.

items.title: LoRA on a Budget: Function-Aware Post-Hoc Compression for Adapter Fleets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LoRA on a Budget: Function-Aware Post-Hoc Compression for Adapter Fleets
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a key mechanism for efficiently specializing foundation models into many task- and user-specific variants. Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank-distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA), an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. items.title: MAREval: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Natural Language Recommendation Explanations [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MAREval: A Multi-Agent Framework for Evaluating Natural Language Recommendation Explanations
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating natural language explanations in recommender systems is essential for fostering user trust, transparency, and engagement. However, existing evaluation approaches like human evaluations, while accurate, are resource-intensive and impractical at the scale required by modern recommendation platforms. Also, automated methods using single-agent LLMs suffer from prompt sensitivity and inconsistent outputs. To address these challenges, we propose MAREval, a structured multi-agent framework for evaluating recommendation explanations using large language models. MAREval orchestrates (i) a planner agent that uses a novel Chain of Debate (CoD) prompting strategy to coordinate agent roles and enforce logically consistent evaluation plans; (ii) a moderator agent that regulates discussions by mitigating prompt drift; and (iii) an arbitrator agent that aggregates outputs from multiple evaluation rounds and (iv) a Monte Carlo sampling method, improving robustness and alignment with human judgment. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on both public (TopicalChat) and proprietary recommendation datasets, demonstrating that MAREval outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Comprehensive experiments on a public benchmark and a proprietary e-commerce dataset show that MAREval improves alignment with human judgments over strong singleand multi-agent baselines. Stability analyses indicate substantially lower variability across repeated trials. In a large human-annotation gate, MAREval meets production quality thresholds where prior evaluators fall short, and online A/B testing demonstrates statistically significant improvements in engagement and revenue metrics. These results establish MAREval as a scalable and reliable solution for human-aligned evaluation of recommendation explanations in real-world systems

items.title: kw-bench: Breaking Frontier Harnesses on Real-World Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: kw-bench: Breaking Frontier Harnesses on Real-World Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Each new generation of frontier model pushes the edge of what is possible. Inside a harness -- a loop, a shell, a filesystem, the ability to write and run its own code -- a model can take on increasingly difficult work. A growing body of work treats the coding-agent harness as infrastructure for knowledge work rather than a coding tool, and a new wave of benchmarks tests it there. Most of them are generative: build a financial model, a memo, a spreadsheet from a brief, judged by a rubric or by another model. Few test the expensive part of knowledge work, which is investigative. In audit, tax, due diligence, regulatory reporting, claims or any dispute over numbers, the answer already exists -- hidden in incomplete and inconsistent evidence spread across systems -- and has to be recovered and defended to the cent. We introduce kw-bench, a benchmark built from real engagements specialists described to us. Its first task family is a five-year VAT reconstruction across three generations of SAP -- legacy ECC, a partial S/4HANA migration and a consultant's redesign -- delivered as raw system extracts: page headers, local number formats, partial link tables, no documentation of how anything connects. Grading is deterministic, with no LLM judge. We ran four harnesses -- Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and micro-cc -- on the same model, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, for two hours. The two independent, model-agnostic harnesses delivered (OpenCode 0.542, micro-cc 0.528); the two lab harnesses, away from their home model, delivered nothing (0.00 each). What defeated them was inertia: keeping many weak signals alive across a long session. On a frontier model the task collapses. micro-cc and Claude Code on Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.9986 and 1.000, in 22 and 25 minutes. A weeks-long engagement now costs minutes and a few dollars; below the frontier, the harness decides how far a model gets.

items.title: Verifiable Efficiency Limits of Innate LLM Planning in Sliding Puzzles [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Verifiable Efficiency Limits of Innate LLM Planning in Sliding Puzzles
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-assisted planning success can reflect external search and verification, leaving a model's unaided planning ability unresolved. We isolate innate planning through complete plans generated in one response without tools or execution feedback. We propose a verifiable framework that decomposes success-weighted plan efficiency as $\mathrm{SPE}=R\times Q\times E$: execution reliability, planning coordination among legal plans, and action economy among completed plans. Trajectory replay and certified optima verify these factors; the joint score includes unsuccessful attempts. We evaluate 8,400 full-plan outputs from seven model conditions on $4\times4$ sliding puzzles, controlling exact horizon and obstacle count in the primary cohort. Models that complete every trial still become less economical at longer horizons, while higher efficiency among completed plans can coexist with poor goal attainment. SPE separates the overall capability hierarchy, while its factors distinguish coordination failure from inefficient completion. The framework makes long-horizon limitations in unaided planning quantitatively verifiable.

items.title: LM-DSB: A Lightweight Multi-agent System for Automated Daily Safety Bulletin Generation in Construction [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LM-DSB: A Lightweight Multi-agent System for Automated Daily Safety Bulletin Generation in Construction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Construction safety management still struggles to produce daily safety bulletins (DSBs), structured daily communications that identify site-specific hazards, convey safety protocols, and set preventive measures for workers. Manual DSB creation takes 2-3 hours daily and yields inconsistent quality, with 25% of crews never conducting pretask planning (Olson et al., 2016), diverting safety personnel from field supervision. This study proposes the Lightweight Multi-Agent DSB System (LM-DSB), which integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a locally deployable Large Language Model (LLM) to automate DSB generation on consumer-grade personal computers. LM-DSB coordinates specialized planner, researcher, and writer agents in a hierarchical architecture, enhanced by domain-specific fine-tuning on construction safety documentation and RAG grounding in 37 health, safety, and environment (HSE) documents. A two-phase validation assessed feasibility. Phase 1 comparative evaluation showed the multi-agent RAG system (Llama 3-8B) outperformed all alternative configurations, with strong lexical alignment and coherence (TF-IDF: 0.70, BLEU: 0.39, ROUGE-1: 0.66) and near-complete document generation (length ratio: 1.01 vs. 0.39 for single-agent RAG). Phase 2 expert evaluation (N=40) confirmed practical acceptability (mean scores 3.50-4.20 on a 5-point scale), particularly in regulatory compliance (4.20) and factual accuracy (4.10). The findings show that architectural design enables lightweight models to handle safety-critical documentation on consumer-grade hardware, advancing technology democratization in construction safety management. Limitations include knowledge base scope, language constraints, and lack of field deployment validation; future work should address multimodal integration and workflow adoption.

items.title: Your Agent Acts Differently When You're Around: How User Presence Changes Agent Behavior in Negotiation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Your Agent Acts Differently When You're Around: How User Presence Changes Agent Behavior in Negotiation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly interact with other agents on behalf of users, yet how users in the loop affect their agents' behavior--for better or worse--remains poorly understood. We study this question through the lens of negotiation, where agents must represent users while strategically bargaining with other agents. To isolate the effect of user presence, we develop PRESENT, a controlled evaluation framework that compares negotiation settings with and without an interactive user, while holding the game, objectives, and user preferences fixed across conditions. Across 11.2k runs spanning 7 games and 8 models, we find that user presence significantly changes both outcomes and behavior. items.title: RouteDRAG: Learning to Route and Control Agentic Execution for Multimodal Document RAG [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RouteDRAG: Learning to Route and Control Agentic Execution for Multimodal Document RAG
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web-based applications increasingly rely on understanding long multimodal documents, where answering questions often requires combining information across pages, tables, and figures. Agentic retrieval-augmented generation addresses these tasks through iterative retrieval and reasoning. However, Agentic execution is not always necessary, introducing additional computation and potentially incorrect answers. Our empirical analysis reveals that Agentic execution provides query-dependent benefits, while additional operations may improve, preserve, or degrade answer accuracy. These findings motivate controlling both Agent invocation and subsequent execution. To address these challenges, we propose RouteDRAG, a learning-based framework comprising four components. Unified Document Index organizes multimodal content into a graph-backed index and derives query representations from initial retrieval. Adaptive Path Routing preserves exact answering and predicts the relative benefit of Agent over shorter execution paths. Dynamic Agent Execution maintains an evolving workspace and refines Planner proposals to control tool use and termination. Sequential Policy Learning first trains operation control from observed outcomes and then trains path routing using the resulting Agent's performance. Across two benchmarks, RouteDRAG achieves an average accuracy improvement of 3.47 percentage points over shorter-path-only execution while assigning only 79.3% of queries to Agent. Notably, it also surpasses uniform Agent execution on both benchmarks while requiring fewer answering calls. Our code is now available at https://github.com/Ereshkigal1/RouteDRAG.

items.title: From Solver Trajectories to Teaching Trajectories: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Solver Trajectories to Teaching Trajectories: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation from large reasoning models (LRMs) often uses raw teacher trajectories as supervision. However, this practice creates a mismatch between the goal of distillation and the nature of teacher trajectories. Advanced LRMs typically improve their reasoning capabilities through reward-driven post-training, such as RLHF. This training optimizes them as strong solvers, rather than as teachers that produce reasoning processes smaller models can easily learn. Since smaller models have different "cognitive capacities" compared to their larger teachers, directly imitating raw teacher trajectories can sometimes be ineffective and often requires a substantial number of high-quality samples. To bridge this mismatch, we propose Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation (CARD), an RL-based framework that transforms solver trajectories into teaching trajectories aligned with the student's cognition. Avoiding expensive resampling, our framework directly transforms existing trajectories. We optimize CARD with two reward signals: (1) a Distribution Alignment Reward that matches the student's predictive distribution, and (2) a Logical Coherence Reward that reduces misleading failed reasoning steps. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple student models and settings demonstrate that CARD outperforms distillation from raw teacher trajectories in in-domain settings while achieving substantial gains in out-of-distribution performance. Code is available at https://github.com/LiteSSLHub/CARD.

items.title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.

items.title: Correction or Manipulation? Measuring Epistemic Vigilance in LLM Agents Under User Pressure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Correction or Manipulation? Measuring Epistemic Vigilance in LLM Agents Under User Pressure
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents that answer questions and act on behalf of users must decide when to yield to a user who disagrees. Disagreement may correct a genuine error or may be an attempt at manipulation. Prior work shows that models frequently abandon correct answers when challenged by users, yet it remains unclear whether they distinguish correction from manipulation or merely differ in their propensity to concede. We examine this question across seven LLMs from four vendors in two studies, one on the answers agents give and one on the actions they take as customer-support agents whose policy permits account changes only for verified users. Simulated users push toward correct and incorrect answers with graded pressure. Following research on epistemic vigilance, the pressure either appeals to the source, such as claimed authority, or offers content the agent cannot verify, namely a cited source. Drawing on signal detection theory, we measure on a set of benchmark questions how much more readily each agent concedes to correction than to manipulation, separately from its overall propensity to concede. Citations made five of seven models readier to concede and four worse at discriminating, while stronger wording added little. In the agentic study, five models never violated the verification policy, including models that readily abandoned correct answers, so concession on answers did not predict violations of policy. Ministral 3B violated the policy mainly under claimed authority, and Ministral 8B reported changes it had not made. An instruction to revise only on verifiable evidence chiefly shifted propensity to concede rather than improving discrimination. Concession rates alone are therefore misleading, and agents should be evaluated on both their discrimination and the actions they take.

items.title: When to Intervene? An Empirical Study of Errors and Self-Recovery in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When to Intervene? An Empirical Study of Errors and Self-Recovery in LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents interact with Web services to perform tasks on users' behalf. Errors during these interactions can disrupt execution and prevent task completion, motivating external intervention. However, agents may self-recover through continued execution, raising the question of when to intervene and when to wait for self-recovery. We present an empirical study of errors and self-recovery in LLM agents. We construct ReInBench, a dataset containing 1,259 agent traces and 1,403 error events across computer-use and Web tasks. Our study examines how often and how quickly agents self-recover, how self-recovery relates to subsequent execution and task completion, and whether self-recovery can be predicted when an error occurs. We find that 725 error events self-recover, often within a few steps, with self-recovery performance differing across Execution LLMs. Self-recovery can also help agents recover from subsequent errors of the same type and support overall task completion. Intervention should therefore prioritize errors unlikely to self-recover, while allowing agents to continue when self-recovery is likely. Building on these empirical findings, we propose ReCoF, a method that predicts whether an error will self-recover to inform whether additional intervention is needed. ReCoF achieves an average relative improvement of 9.02% in Macro-F1 over the strongest baseline on ReInBench. Our code and data can be found at https://method-notes.github.io/ReCoF/.

items.title: CogArena: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents on Interactive Behavioral Experiments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CogArena: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents on Interactive Behavioral Experiments
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.

items.title: AC-JEPA: Anchored Cross-Modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Visual-to-Symbolic Translation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AC-JEPA: Anchored Cross-Modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Visual-to-Symbolic Translation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-modal translation requires models to capture shared semantics across modalities while preserving the fine-grained structure required by the target modality. Yet in real-world scientific domains, paired data are often imperfect, while obtaining clean pairs at scale is costly. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) directly optimizes cross-modal translation through categorical token-level supervision, but this objective is sensitive to errors in the target sequences. JEPA offers a complementary representation-space objective, but most existing formulations focus on prediction within a modality rather than translation across modalities. We introduce Anchored Cross-Modal JEPA (AC-JEPA), an SFT-compatible plug-in that predicts masked intermediate states in both cross-modal directions using paired data. The joint-embedding objective targets cross-modal structure predictable from context, while the causal SFT path retains direct token-level supervision for the target sequence. During self-training, AC-JEPA learns from continuous latent targets derived from imperfect pseudo-labeled pairs, offering intrinsic tolerance to local data errors without promoting pseudo-tokens to hard categorical supervision. Using optical chemical structure recognition as a testbed, AC-JEPA trained on clean pairs achieves 76.07% accuracy on the Simple set of the WildMol benchmark, compared with 67.40% for SFT alone. Using the same pseudo-labeled data for both approaches, AC-JEPA-based self-training further raises accuracy to 80.23%, whereas accuracy under direct SFT drops from 67.40% to 63.47%. These results support SFT-anchored joint-embedding prediction as an effective strategy for cross-modal translation under both curated and imperfect supervision.

items.title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.
